records.name_note: Admissible sources split three ways on which common name leads, and each is a dedicated single-species profile (the cited NC State slug is the canonical /anacis-tripteris/). NC State's 'Common Name(s):' field is a stacked, alphabetized three-entry list (Golden Crown, Tall Coreopsis, Tall Tickseed) whose order alone marks no primary; NC State's own body prose uses 'Tall coreopsis' three times ('Tall coreopsis is a very tall, native herbaceous perennial...', 'Tall coreopsis is low-maintenance, hardy, easy to grow...', 'Consider the tall coreopsis for naturalization in meadows or wildflower gardens.'). MoBot's displayed 'Common Name:' field reads 'tickseed', which MoBot's own prose identifies as a genus-umbrella name ('Plants in the genus Coreopsis are sometimes commonly called tickseed...'), so that field is set aside; MoBot's species prose leads with the same name NC State's prose uses ('Coreopsis tripteris, commonly called tall coreopsis or tall tickseed...'), and its Common Names tooltip lists tickseed, golden crown, tall coreopsis, tall tickseed. RHS's plant-profile subtitle and page title read 'golden crown', with no Other common names field on this page. common_name is Golden Crown: once MoBot's umbrella field is set aside it is the only affirmative structured lead designation among the three dedicated pages (RHS's subtitle), and it also heads NC State's list. 'Tall Coreopsis' is the name both NC State's and MoBot's running prose actually use, and 'Tall Tickseed' is a sourced alternate; neither is an error. Taxonomy: the species was moved out of Coreopsis in 2024. NC State gives Anacis tripteris as the accepted binomial (its H1 and scientific name), lists Coreopsis tripteris under 'Previously known as:', and says the plant was formerly known as Coreopsis tripteris; RHS's Name Status field still marks Coreopsis tripteris itself 'Correct' -- a lag in adoption rather than a symmetric disagreement. scientific_name_accepted follows NC State's stated accepted binomial, as this catalog did for garden pea (Lathyrus oleraceus, b11).
unknowns: RHS's Position field lists 'Full sun, Partial shade' for this species, but neither NC State's structured Light field (Full sun only) nor MoBot's structured Sun field (Full sun only) corroborates partial shade, so part_shade was left out of outdoor_sun_exposure per the rule that a value excluded by two of three sources' structured sun fields is disclosed rather than included.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max were left null: NC State's closed 'Neutral (6.0-8.0)' band would otherwise set a 6.0 floor and 8.0 ceiling, but RHS's Soil pH field lists 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral' as all acceptable — since RHS accepts alkaline soils the ceiling is dropped, and since RHS accepts acid soils the floor is dropped too, per the two-directional check rule.

chill_damage_f, cool_rest_note, day/night temperature fields, humidity_pct fields, and light_fc fields have no admissible-source support for Coreopsis tripteris — no source states a numeric damage-onset temperature, indoor day/night range, humidity percentage, or foot-candle figure for this outdoor prairie/woodland-margin perennial, so all were left null.

humidity_need was left null: MoBot's Culture text says the plant is 'Tolerant of heat, humidity and drought,' which is a tolerance statement, not a stated humidity requirement/preference level (low/average/high), so it does not support a specific enum value.

direct_sun_hours_max was left null: NC State's only hour figure ('6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day') comes from its site-wide Light-category legend attached to the 'Full sun' tag, not species-specific prose, so per the rules it cannot be used to populate this field.

water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, and water_dormant_days_est were left null: this is an in-ground garden/prairie perennial and no admissible source frames its watering in dry-down-depth or day-interval terms.
fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, and fertilize_strength were left null: none of NC State, MoBot, or RHS mentions fertilizing this species at all.

is_houseplant was inferred as false from the absence of any indoor/houseplant framing and the uniform outdoor hardiness-zone/garden-use framing across all three sources; no source states 'houseplant' or 'indoor' literally for this species.

toxicity_detail was left null: NC State's Plant Type list for this species does not include 'Poisonous' and its Problems/tag set does not include 'Poisonous to Humans,' so there is no Poison block on the page to report; the non-toxic-for-cats/dogs/horses tags speak only to toxic_to_pets, not to a symptom/severity/poison-part narrative.

water_regime was set to dry_surface_between from MoBot's structured 'Water: Dry to medium' field and its Culture-section cultivation prose ('Easily grown in dry to medium moisture, well-drained soil'); NC State's body-prose phrasing 'medium-moist, medium-dry, well-drained soil of most soil types' is a looser, non-structured echo of the same dry-to-medium characterization and was treated as consistent rather than conflicting.

records.name_note: Admissible sources genuinely split three ways on the lead common name (Clustered / Short-toothed / Blunt). NC State's Common Name(s) field lists three names in alphabetical order, with 'Blunt Mountain Mint' first; NC State's page title leads with the same name, and its Description prose uses it throughout. Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder shows an affirmative 'Common Name: blunt mountainmint' field, with a longer Common Names tooltip behind it (blunt mountainmint, mountain mint, clustered mountainmint, blunt mountain mint); MoBot's Noteworthy Characteristics prose introduces the plant as 'commonly called mountain mint or short-toothed mountain mint or clustered mountain mint', never using 'blunt' as a common name, though the same section's etymology line notes the epithet means 'blunt' -- so MoBot's structured Common Name field and its prose emphasize different names from the same four-name set. RHS's plant-profile subtitle and page title name it 'short-toothed mountain mint', with 'big leaf mountain mint' and 'clustered mountain mint' appearing only in RHS's separate 'Other common names' field. Penn State Extension's dedicated single-species rain-garden page is titled and headed 'Clustered Mountain Mint'. Two of the four admissible dedicated single-species pages (NC State, structurally and in prose; MoBot's structured Common Name field) converge on 'Blunt Mountain Mint', which is why it was selected; RHS and Penn State Extension each lead with a different name.

RHS, by contrast, gives its plant-profile subtitle and page title as 'American wild bergamot' rather than plain 'wild bergamot.' Because NC State's own prose, MoBot's primary field, and UMD's page all converge on 'wild bergamot,' that name (title-cased as Wild Bergamot) is used as common_name, with RHS's divergent 'American wild bergamot' noted here.

RHS's cultivation prose instructs 'do not allow to dry out in summer,' while MoBot's structured Water field rates it mid-scale ('Dry to medium'), and NC State/UMD both emphasize drought tolerance in dry, well-drained soils ('tolerant of occasional drought'; 'Plant this in poor, dry soil or you will be punished with stems that cannot support their own growth'). No single enum value can be applied without contradicting at least one source, so this is left null rather than guessed.

This is an in-ground meadow/border perennial rather than a houseplant, so per the schema rules the watering-schedule and day-interval fields are left null absent a source that explicitly frames watering that way.

Clemson HGIC (hgic.clemson.edu) has no dedicated Monarda fistulosa care page — search only surfaced garden-photo blog posts and general Wildflowers/Pollinator Gardening factsheets — so it contributes no species-specific citations here.

Powdery mildew, captured as the sources state it: NC State says 'Powdery mildew can be a problem with all beebalm species, especially in crowded conditions with poor airflow, but this particular species shows resistance. Prune stems to increase air flow. Severe cases may require fungicidal sprays. In addition, if the soil is allowed to dry out, the stressed plants become increasingly susceptible to disease. Rust can also be a problem.' MoBot similarly says 'Powdery mildew can be a significant problem with the monardas, particularly in crowded gardens with poor air circulation. This species has good mildew resistance, however. Rust can also be a problem.' Both describe M. fistulosa as comparatively resistant among Monarda/beebalm species, not immune — neither source was used to set any structured field, since no schema field maps to disease resistance.

UMD Extension's page confirms the 'Wild Bergamot' common name and native Maryland status, and adds a cultivation caution and pollinator/deer-and-rabbit-resistance notes, but gives no numeric watering, pH, or fertilizing guidance, so it did not support any additional numeric fields.

records.name_note: Sources split three ways on which common name leads for Ratibida pinnata. NC State's Common Name(s) field is a six-entry alphabetized list (Drooping Coneflower, Gray-headed Coneflower, Grey-headed Coneflower, Pinnate Prairie Coneflower, Prairie Coneflower, Yellow Coneflower); because it is alphabetized -- and because the page-title parenthetical repeats the identical order -- its ordering is not a lead designation, and NC State's own body prose instead leads with 'Yellow coneflower.' Missouri Botanical Garden carries an affirmative single-line Common Name field reading 'grey-head coneflower', with a hover tooltip listing two names (grey-head coneflower; drooping coneflower); MoBot's own Noteworthy Characteristics prose spells it differently again, as 'gray headed coneflower.' RHS's H1 is the botanical name alone, its subtitle reads 'pinnate prairie coneflower' (its page title being 'Ratibida pinnata | pinnate prairie coneflower'), and 'grey-headed coneflower' and 'yellow coneflower' sit in the secondary Other common names field. No name is the affirmed lead of two of the three pages. This record therefore takes Grey-head Coneflower as common_name, being the only affirmative primary designation among the three (MoBot's labelled Common Name field, also first in its tooltip), following this catalog's precedent of preferring a labelled designation; Gray-headed Coneflower (the usual North American spelling, on NC State's list), Yellow Coneflower (NC State's prose lead, and an RHS Other common name) and Pinnate Prairie Coneflower (RHS's subtitle) are sourced alternates. Both NC State ('Previously known as: Rudbeckia pinnata') and RHS (Synonyms: Rudbeckia pinnata) record the former placement in Rudbeckia.
unknowns: No admissible source (NC State, Missouri Botanical Garden, or RHS) carries a toxicity/poison block for Ratibida pinnata — NC State's page has no Poison Symptoms/Poison Part/Poison Severity fields and no Problems tag of Poisonous to Humans, Cats, or Dogs, and neither MoBot nor RHS mentions toxicity. toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are left null rather than borrowed from genus-level or general Asteraceae knowledge.

outdoor_sun_exposure omits part_shade: NC State's structured Light field lists both Full sun and Partial Shade as accepted, but Missouri Botanical Garden's Sun field and RHS's Position/aspect fields state Full sun only, so part_shade — listed by only one of the three dedicated pages and excluded by the structured sun fields of the other two — is left out per the primacy rule.

direct_sun_hours_max is left null: NC State's only hour figure ("6 or more hours") sits inside its site-wide light-category legend text, not species-specific prose, so it cannot be used per the rule against citing that generic legend range; no other admissible source gives an hour figure.

soil_ph_min/max are left null: RHS's Soil pH field is categorical ("Alkaline or Neutral") with no numeric range given, and NC State's Ratibida pinnata page has no Soil pH field at all to derive a Neutral-band ceiling/floor from, so there is no admissible numeric pH to check RHS against.

water_regime is left null: NC State's cultivation prose only offers a drought-tolerance/don't-overwater caution (not a watering-frequency statement), and Missouri Botanical Garden's structured field reads "Water: Medium," which per rule is mid-scale and cannot on its own support any of the four watering enum values; no source frames watering for this in-ground perennial in dry-down or moisture-retention terms that map to the enum.

water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, and water_estimate_basis are left null: this is an in-ground prairie perennial and no admissible source frames its watering as a container-style dry-down/interval schedule.

fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, and fertilize_strength are left null: the only admissible mention of fertilizer is NC State's caution not to over-fertilize a drought- and poor-soil-tolerant plant — no source gives an interval, active-season months, or a dilution/strength fraction.

chill_damage_f and cool_rest_note are left null: no admissible source states a damage-onset temperature; RHS's H6 rating and NC State's USDA zone 3a–8b range are hardiness/survival ratings, not onset figures, and were not used for this field per the rule against deriving chill damage from a hardiness rating.

day_f_min/max, night_f_min/max, humidity_need, humidity_pct_min/max, and light_fc_min/good are left null: this is an outdoor garden perennial and no admissible source frames its care in indoor day/night temperature, humidity percentage, or foot-candle terms.

hgic.clemson.edu, extension.psu.edu, extension.umd.edu, edis.ifas.ufl.edu, ask.ifas.ufl.edu, and fieldreport.caes.uga.edu do not appear to carry a dedicated Ratibida pinnata species page; searches surfaced only incidental mentions in unrelated publications (e.g., a UMD plant-inventory list, a UF/IFAS butterfly-gardening publication, a UF/IFAS wildflower-liner-production publication), none of which were used as they are not dedicated cultivation pages for this species and were not fetched to confirm exact rendered wording.

This record is for Ratibida pinnata (Gray-headed Coneflower / Yellow Coneflower / Pinnate Prairie Coneflower), confirmed distinct from Ratibida columnifera (Mexican Hat) across all three fetched pages — none of the fetched content described R. columnifera.

records.name_note: Admissible sources split on the lead common name, and the plain name 'Blue Star' is the genus-level umbrella: Clemson's Bluestar article opens on the genus Amsonia, NC State's page for Amsonia tabernaemontana carries 'Blue Star' in its own common-name list, and MoBot's Common Name field for that species is also 'blue star' -- so 'Blue Star' would collide with Eastern Bluestar, already in this catalog. NC State's species page lists five common names alphabetically under 'Common Name(s):' (Arkansas Amsonia, Blue Star, Blue Star Amsonia, Hubricht's Amsonia, Threadleaf Blue Star) with Arkansas Amsonia first and the same order in its page title; NC State's own body prose opens with 'Blue star.' NC State auto-generates an alias page for each of the five listed names (e.g. /common-name/threadeaf-blue-star/, H1 'Threadleaf Blue Star'), so those pages are symmetric and carry no primacy signal in either direction. Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder displays 'Common Name: blue star' (with no Common Names list behind it on this page), but MoBot's own Noteworthy Characteristics prose contradicts that field: 'Amsonia hubrichtii, commonly called threadleaf bluestar or Hubricht's bluestar...'. RHS's H1 is the bare binomial 'Amsonia hubrichtii,' with 'Arkansas bluestar' as the plant-profile subtitle and page-title common name, and 'Hubricht's bluestar' listed separately under 'Other common names.' Clemson HGIC's Bluestar article, which specifically profiles this species alongside Amsonia tabernaemontana, refers to it as 'Threadleaf' or 'Hubricht's Bluestar.' Applying the lead test to the three dedicated pages: NC State leads with Arkansas Amsonia, RHS with Arkansas bluestar, and only MoBot with blue star -- two of three for an Arkansas name. common_name is Arkansas Bluestar (RHS's lead, NC State's cognate first entry, and the catalog's own subject name); Threadleaf Bluestar and Hubricht's Bluestar (MoBot prose, Clemson, RHS Other common names) are species-distinguishing alternates.
records.toxicity_detail: Clemson HGIC's genus-level Bluestar article — which specifically profiles Amsonia hubrichtii by name ("Threadleaf or Hubricht's Bluestar") alongside Amsonia tabernaemontana — states that Amsonia's milky sap is toxic to dogs: "All are in the Apocynaceae (Dogbane) family, so named because the milky sap is slightly toxic to dogs." This is a genus-wide characterization rather than a statement scoped only to A. hubrichtii, and no cat-specific toxicity statement was found in any admissible source. Separately, NC State's species page carries only a human-directed handling caution, not a structured Poison block: "Caution should be used when cutting back, as the milky white sap can cause skin irritation." NC State's Plant Type field for this species lists only "Herbaceous Perennial," with no "Poisonous" tag, and no Problems tags carrying "Poisonous to Humans," "Poisonous to Cats," or "Poisonous to Dogs" were present on the page.
unknowns: No admissible source stated a chill-damage onset temperature, a day/night temperature range, a humidity requirement or percentage range, light in foot-candles, or a species-specific maximum direct-sun-hours figure for Amsonia hubrichtii; these fields are left null.
No admissible source addressed a fertilizing interval, active months, or dilution strength for this species; fertilize fields are left null.

MoBot's Plant Finder carries a structured 'Water: Medium' field for this species, which per scoring rules is mid-scale and does not itself support any water_regime enum value; no watering statement or moisture field mapping cleanly to keep_moist/keep_barely_moist/dry_surface_between/dry_thoroughly_between was found, so water_regime is left null and this counterpoint is disclosed here.
